title: Xuanzang at Nalanda
hook: after deserts and mountains, the traveler sits down and becomes a student again

segments.voice: Yesterday, Xuanzang crossed the desert, lost his water, and turned his horse west again. Your line: alone across the sand. What was the first step you took? Day nine hundred eight.

What does a person do after crossing deserts and mountain passes to reach the place he set out for? Throw a party? Write home? Xuanzang became a student again. He reached Nalanda, the great monastery of learning in north India that we visited earlier this year, and instead of collecting texts and hurrying back, he stayed. He learned the language. He sat in lectures. He read the same difficult books over and over. Earlier we saw Nalanda as a place. Today we see it through one pair of eyes, a guest from China who made it his school.
screen: `THE TRAVELER ARRIVES.` → `HE STAYS.` → `NALANDA THROUGH ONE PAIR OF EYES.`

segments.voice: First, the teacher who was waiting. The head of Nalanda in Xuanzang's day was an old monk named Shilabhadra, deeply honored there, his biography says. And it tells a striking story: years before, Shilabhadra had been ill and in pain, and in a dream he was told to bear it, because a monk from China would come to learn from him. When Xuanzang arrived, the story of that dream was told to him. Second, what he came to learn. Shilabhadra taught the Yogacara, a school whose great subject is the mind: how what we experience is shaped by the mind that experiences it. Xuanzang had come for one long text of that school in particular, and he heard it taught through from beginning to end. Third, life inside the walls. The biography describes monks discussing and debating from morning until night, rooms given to guests, and food supplied so the students could study. Xuanzang learned Sanskrit well enough to read, argue and later translate. Fourth, why it matters. He could have filled his bags and left. He didn't. He stayed for years, because some things don't open on a first reading. The Dhammapada, the Buddha's sayings, begins with a line that points the same way: "All that we are is the result of what we have thought." A line like that is easy to say and slow to understand. Depth can look like this: coming back to the same thing until it gives up what it has.
screen: `AN OLD TEACHER WAITING.` · `A SCHOOL ABOUT THE MIND.` · `DEBATE FROM MORNING TO NIGHT.` · `STAYING UNTIL IT OPENS.` · then, large: `YEARS AT NALANDA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: study one thing deeply. Sit comfortably and let the breath slow. Take the line from today: all that we are is the result of what we have thought. Say it once, silently. Then take just the first half, all that we are, and let it sit. Then the second half. Notice one thought passing through you right now, and ask, gently, what it's making of this moment. When the mind drifts, come back to the line. One line, many times. The bell holds the time.
Xuanzang at Nalanda. The traveler who arrived and then sat down to learn, with an old teacher who had been waiting for him. Today's word.
Your line: years at Nalanda. Today, pick one thing you've only skimmed, a page, a song, a recipe, and give it a few unhurried minutes. Day nine hundred eight.

howItsDone: In monastic schools of several Buddhist traditions, students still study a few core texts slowly with a teacher, memorizing, discussing and debating them.

notes: Dhammapada 1 quoted from Max Müller (1881); confirm exact wording.
'Deeply honored there, his biography says': confirm the Life presents Shilabhadra this way; soften if not.
Shilabhadra's dream (told to bear his illness because a monk from China would come) and his weeping at Xuanzang's arrival: from Huili's Life, book 3; confirm.
'Yogacara, a school whose name means the practice of yoga': confirm this gloss is acceptable; the 'one long text' is the Yogacarabhumi, left unnamed on purpose.
No count of years given; the index says 'years'.
Debating from morning until night, rooms and food for guests: from the Life's description of Nalanda; confirm.
